title: Can Dubai caterers accommodate nut and shellfish allergies?
body_markdown:
Nut and shellfish allergies require case-by-case confirmation from your Dubai caterer, not simply a menu without those ingredients. Before booking, ask whether the kitchen can control cross-contact during preparation, transport and service. A dish described as containing no nuts or shellfish is not automatically suitable for someone with an allergy.


**TL;DR**

- Nut allergy catering in Dubai requires ingredient checks and cross-contact controls, not just menu substitutions.
- Ask your caterer to confirm the exact allergens, preparation arrangements and serving responsibilities in writing.
- myCHEF provides event catering; discuss allergy requirements before treating any proposed menu as suitable.
- If the kitchen cannot explain its controls, do not assume the meal meets the guest’s requirements.


## Can Dubai caterers accommodate nut and shellfish allergies?

**Accommodation depends on the caterer’s confirmed process, not the cuisine, venue or event size.** You need an answer covering ingredients, shared equipment and the journey from kitchen to guest. A reassuring conversation is useful; a clear written plan is more useful.

Start by establishing who supplies the ingredients and equipment. The guide to [whether private chefs bring groceries and equipment](https://www.mychef.ae/blog/do-private-chefs-in-dubai-bring-their-own-groceries-and-equipment) covers a practical question to resolve before discussing preparation in your home.

Use this sequence when assessing a catering proposal:

1. **Identify the exact allergens.** Record the guest’s stated requirements rather than writing only ‘dietary restrictions’.
2. **Review the complete menu.** Include sauces, garnishes, desserts, drinks and any food supplied by someone else.
3. **Ask about cross-contact.** Establish how ingredients, utensils, preparation surfaces and serving equipment will be handled.
4. **Confirm the handover.** Name the person responsible for identifying and delivering the agreed meal.
5. **Record the limits.** Ask the caterer to state what it cannot accommodate before you accept the proposal.

Do not make the host responsible for interpreting an unclear answer. Bring the guest into the discussion, with their permission, whenever their requirements need clarification.

## Why removing an ingredient is not enough

Cross-contact occurs when an allergen unintentionally transfers to another food. Shared utensils, preparation surfaces and cooking equipment can introduce an allergen even when it is absent from the recipe. Food Allergy Research & Education describes cross-contact as a separate concern from a food’s intended ingredients.

For your event, that distinction changes the questions you ask. ‘Can you leave off the pistachios?’ addresses the recipe. ‘How will you prepare, plate and serve this dish without contact with pistachios?’ addresses the process.

Do not accept removing a garnish from an already prepared dish as the agreed solution. The caterer needs to assess the whole dish and preparation method. The guest should not have to inspect the plate and decide whether it looks suitable.

**A menu omission is not an allergy-control plan.** Keep that distinction clear when comparing proposals, especially when a supplier uses broad descriptions such as ‘allergy-friendly’ without explaining what they mean.

## What information should you give the caterer?

Provide a written allergy brief before menu design. Keep it separate from preferences such as avoiding spicy food, so the operational requirements are not lost among optional requests.

### Name the foods precisely

Peanuts and tree nuts are different allergens. Shellfish and fish are also different categories; shellfish includes crustaceans and molluscs. Do not substitute a broad label for the guest’s own confirmed requirements.

Ask the guest which foods they must avoid and pass that information on accurately. Do not infer that someone who avoids prawns can eat mussels, or that avoiding almonds describes every nut-related restriction they have.

### Explain the service setting

Tell the caterer whether preparation will happen in a production kitchen, your home or the venue. Describe the available kitchen, shared storage and any other food being served. For a Dubai apartment or villa, include building access and kitchen access arrangements in the practical brief.

Also mention outside suppliers. A birthday cake, sweets brought by relatives or snacks already on the table belong in the discussion, even if the caterer is not responsible for producing them.

### Agree how information will be shared

Give the caterer a named contact for questions and ask who will brief the kitchen and service team. Share health information only with the people who need it and with the guest’s agreement.

If you enquire with myCHEF about event catering, include the allergy requirements alongside the date, location, guest count and service format. Ask for confirmation of suitability rather than assuming that a tailored menu resolves every concern.

## Which catering format makes allergy communication easier?

No service format guarantees an allergy-safe meal. Compare where control sits, who handles the food and how the agreed dish reaches the right person. Choose the format only after the caterer confirms that its preparation and service arrangements meet the brief.

| Service format | Best for | Practical advantage | Limitation to resolve |
|---|---|---|---|
| Individually plated service | A clearly assigned meal and named recipient | Allows an agreed plate-to-guest handover | Kitchen controls and correct identification still need confirmation |
| Staffed buffet | Events needing a shared display with service support | Staff can manage serving utensils and answer menu questions | Shared dishes and guest movement create additional handling points |
| Drop-off catering | Hosts who can take responsibility after delivery | Provides a defined delivery and handover point | The host must maintain the agreed separation and identification |
| Chef cooking on site | Hosts wanting preparation arrangements discussed directly | Allows the working kitchen and equipment to be reviewed | A domestic kitchen is not automatically free from allergens |

**Best for a clear handover: individually plated service, provided the preparation process is suitable.** This is a logistical advantage, not a medical assurance. A separately plated meal prepared without adequate controls does not solve the underlying problem.

For a buffet, ask whether an individually prepared and identified meal is possible instead of expecting the guest to select from shared trays. For drop-off service, confirm what happens after the delivery team leaves.

## Why accommodation varies between events

The same menu request can involve different practical arrangements at different venues. Assess the actual event rather than relying on a caterer’s answer from a previous booking.

- **Ingredient sourcing:** The kitchen needs to review the ingredients and relevant supplier information for the proposed dishes.
- **Shared preparation:** Ask which equipment and working areas are shared, and what controls apply.
- **Menu complexity:** Sauces, garnishes and outsourced components each need consideration, not just the main ingredient.
- **Service format:** Plated meals, shared buffets and drop-off food create different handover responsibilities.
- **Venue arrangements:** Kitchen access, storage and other food suppliers affect how the agreed process is carried out.
- **Changes after approval:** A replacement ingredient, altered dish or additional supplier needs a fresh check before service.

Ask for a proposal that identifies these responsibilities. An extra member of serving staff, for example, does not by itself establish that the kitchen can accommodate the allergy. Staffing and preparation controls answer different questions.

## What should the written confirmation cover?

Written confirmation should describe the agreed arrangements and their limits. It is not a substitute for appropriate kitchen practice, but it gives the host, caterer and guest a shared reference.

Use these headings when requesting a response:

- **Allergen brief:** The exact foods the guest has identified.
- **Ingredient review:** Who checks recipes, purchased components and substitutions.
- **Preparation controls:** How equipment, surfaces and working areas will be managed.
- **Service handover:** How the meal will be identified and delivered.
- **Change approval:** Who must be consulted before an ingredient or dish changes.


![Checklist covering the allergy brief, ingredient review, preparation controls, service handover and changes](https://gwvckixiegkllthleuyt.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/workspace-article-images-public/b09bf892-4fd0-4e03-a33c-cb919cd3c6eb/body-c8114c37d2e59ff183d8ed29d8c78dca.jpg)

*Confirm the full process, not just the dish name.*


Ask the caterer to explain any limitation in plain language. ‘We cannot provide separate preparation equipment’ is actionable information. An undefined promise to ‘take extra care’ leaves you without a basis for deciding.

If the answer remains unclear, pause confirmation of the affected meal. Ask the guest to review the response and decide whether it meets their requirements. Do not pressure them to accept an arrangement because the wider event menu has already been chosen.

## How should you plan the menu?

Build the menu around dishes the kitchen can explain fully. Familiar dish names are not enough: recipes differ, and sauces or garnishes can change the ingredient list. Ask about every component rather than making assumptions based on cuisine.

For example, an illustrative menu might include a plainly prepared main course, vegetables and a separately discussed dessert. That is a starting point for a conversation, not an approved allergy menu. Each ingredient and preparation step still needs confirmation.

Check these easily overlooked components:

- Dressings, marinades, stocks and finishing sauces.
- Bread, pastries, confectionery and dessert decorations.
- Oils, spice mixtures and purchased condiments.
- Drinks with garnishes or added ingredients.
- Food supplied by a venue, bakery or guest.

Avoid treating ‘vegan’, ‘halal’ or ‘gluten-free’ as shorthand for suitability for nut or shellfish allergies. Those descriptions answer different questions. The caterer must assess the specific allergy brief regardless of the menu’s other dietary descriptions.

## Who takes responsibility on the event day?

Agree the handover before guests arrive. The host should know who answers ingredient questions, who identifies the agreed meal and who authorises changes. Serving staff need the final brief, not an earlier menu draft.

For a shared table, discuss where the guest’s meal will be placed and how serving utensils will be managed. For a catered office event, make sure the person receiving delivery has the same instructions as the person who placed the order.

Keep the guest’s own emergency plan separate from the catering plan. Catering arrangements do not replace prescribed medication or medical advice. If a serious allergic reaction is suspected, seek emergency medical assistance immediately and follow the person’s prescribed emergency instructions.

The host’s role is coordination, not medical assessment. Do not ask a guest to try a small amount to see whether a dish is suitable.

## FAQ


**Can a Dubai caterer guarantee that a meal is nut-free?**

Do not assume a guarantee from a menu description. Ask the caterer to explain its ingredient checks, shared-kitchen arrangements and limitations, then let the guest assess whether the response meets their requirements.

**Is removing prawns enough for someone with a shellfish allergy?**

Removing prawns does not establish that a dish is suitable for someone with a shellfish allergy. Other ingredients and contact during preparation or service also need assessment.

**Should I tell the caterer about an allergy before choosing the menu?**

Yes, provide the allergy brief before menu design. The caterer needs to assess ingredients and preparation arrangements before proposing suitable dishes.

**Is plated catering better than a buffet for an allergic guest?**

Plated catering offers a clearer meal-to-guest handover, but it does not guarantee suitable preparation. A buffet adds shared serving points that also need to be addressed.

**Can a private chef use my home kitchen for an allergy-specific meal?**

A private chef must assess the home kitchen and proposed process before confirming suitability. Shared equipment, stored ingredients and other food preparation still need discussion.

**Does halal catering mean a meal is suitable for nut allergies?**

Halal catering does not establish suitability for nut allergies. Ask separately about the exact allergens, ingredients and cross-contact controls.

**Can myCHEF discuss allergy requirements for an event?**

Include allergy requirements when enquiring about myCHEF event catering. Request explicit confirmation of the proposed arrangements and limitations before treating a menu as suitable.

- [Can catering companies provide serving staff and cleanup?](https://www.mychef.ae/blog/can-catering-companies-in-dubai-provide-serving-staff-and-cleanup)
- [From guest list to plated dinner: planning the event workflow](https://www.mychef.ae/blog/guest-list-to-plated-dinner-private-chef-event-workflow)

## Before you confirm the menu

Ask who can stop a substitution on the day. A carefully reviewed menu loses its value if someone changes a sauce or garnish without checking the allergy brief. Make change approval part of the service instructions, not an informal request.

For a myCHEF catering enquiry, send your date, Dubai location, guest count and service required, together with the exact allergy requirements. Ask for a proposed menu and a clear explanation of what can and cannot be accommodated before you confirm.
